extracted.intended_audience: student reporters and working newspaper reporters (news writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing news stories based on speeches, lectures, addresses, sermons, interviews and written reports, focusing on accuracy, condensation, treatment, and use of human-interest detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of the type of story
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches, lectures, addresses, and sermons may be considered in the same class with interviews and reports, because all are alike in being some form of utterance. A speech and a report differ only in the fact that one is spoken and the other is written. An interview, likewise, may be regarded as an informal address delivered to an audience of one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat news stories of these forms largely as reproductions of the words and ideas of a person; anticipate that such stories will consist chiefly of direct and indirect quotations and that the writing task is mainly to present those utterances clearly and accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose — accuracy of reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: To reproduce as accurately as possible the ideas expressed by a speaker, by a person interviewed, or by the author of a report is obviously the only object in writing a news story dealing with such material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All quotation, direct or indirect, should be accurate not only in substance and form but also in spirit. The writer must avoid carelessness in taking down what is said, avoid giving disproportionate space or emphasis to some points, and avoid misrepresentation from partisanship or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of quotation: substance, form, and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: All quotation, direct or indirect, should be accurate not only in substance and form but also in spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement taken verbatim may be played up in the lead in such a way that it does not give the actual thought or purpose of the original; maintain context when using verbatim material and ensure the quoted wording genuinely reflects the speaker's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding distortion and suppression (ethical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distortion and suppression of speeches, interviews, or reports because of political or other bias is indefensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not selectively omit, alter, or emphasize parts of an utterance to fit a partisan viewpoint. Present a balanced representation of the speaker's main points and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common faults to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Four common faults that endanger the accuracy of news stories of this type are carelessness in taking down what is said, the playing up of statements that taken from their context are misleading, unintentional distortion due to giving disproportionate space or emphasis to some points, and misrepresentation because of political partisanship or other bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be meticulous in recording, resist sensationalizing single phrases out of context, proportion coverage to the speaker’s emphasis, and check for unconscious bias that may skew presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment — condensing and combining material
rubrics_metrics.description: Since news stories of this class must consist largely of direct and indirect quotation from an utterance, the problem of presenting news of this kind is usually that of condensing, summarizing, and combining different parts of the available material into a unified, coherent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillfully select, compress, and sequence quotes and paraphrase to create a coherent narrative or exposition that preserves meaning and proportion; this requires effort and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of human-interest and descriptive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing up interviews and speeches the reporter has a chance to portray clearly and attractively the speaker and the circumstances, thus stimulating the reader’s interest in the utterance. In interviews it is possible to bring out the human interest element in portraying the character and personality of the person interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, include description of the speaker, audience, setting, and manner to add human interest—especially in interviews—while keeping the central aim of accurate reproduction of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling reporter’s questions in interview stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter’s questions, which are a necessary means of obtaining an expression of ideas, are suppressed in many stories. In other stories, the questions are embodied in the answers or are repeated by the person interviewed. There is a growing tendency, particularly in signed stories of interviews, to give the reporter’s questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to suppress, paraphrase, or print questions verbatim based on clarity and usefulness; consider audience expectations and whether including questions improves comprehension or fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads and selection of material — avoid misleading emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement taken verbatim from a speech, interview, or report, may be played up in the lead in such a way that it does not give the actual thought or purpose of the original. By confining his news story to only one or two phases of the subject discussed, a writer often gives an erroneous impression of the whole speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a lead and selecting material, ensure the lead reflects the speaker’s main thrust; avoid selecting striking but unrepresentative quotes as the lead if they distort the overall meaning.
